# What NetAtlas models

Each protocol, service and application profile states what NetAtlas does for
it, at one of three levels: **Diagram only** (drawn and documented),
**Configuration and validation** (its settings are checked; its exchanges are
not simulated) and **Modeled behavior** (the simulation runs its exchanges and
state, within the stated limits; never "full support"). The static analyses
evaluate the configured model or a simulation snapshot and send nothing. The
application shows the same statements in its ⓘ notes and in Help → User
Manual → *What NetAtlas models*. [LIMITATIONS.md](LIMITATIONS.md) adds the
simplifications that cut across them.

## Static analysis (Analyze)

| Analysis | Evaluates | Does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Path tracing (Communication) | Longest-prefix forwarding over connected networks, static routes (distance, metric, recursive next hops) and the routes of enabled routing protocols’ adjacencies through the routing-policy subset (advertised prefixes, a default route, redistribution with its origin history, ordered import/export filters, BGP local preference and AS path); equal-cost paths (up to 16), VRFs, VRRP / HSRP holders, tunnels with their traced underlay, the layer-2 way through VLANs and Wi-Fi networks; the filtering decision of network policies (routers, Layer 3 switches, firewalls) and Security gateways for a given service; NAT of container bridges. | the NAT service’s translations (the simulation applies them), policy-based routing, MPLS label forwarding, multicast forwarding (the simulation forwards multicast), spanning-tree blocking (the cable way is the shortest one through layer-2 devices). |
| Network policy | One engine for Communication, Design review and the simulation: a router’s, Layer 3 switch’s or firewall’s ordered rules (addresses and objects, protocol, ports, interfaces and zones, an explicit default action), the rule that decided named (also for the packets of relations and tunnels through it, and IP protocols without ports by `proto: any` rules and the default action, tracked by address pair and IP protocol number); a firewall without one: its relations and allow list. A rule naming a device: that device’s addresses, checked against the device the traffic reaches (an address several devices have and no owner known: undecided, never permitted). | a return decision statically (the simulation keeps a stateful policy’s sessions); application identification, TLS inspection, user identities, NAT rules, VLAN ACLs. |
| Communication check | Address, name resolution (the model’s DNS zones and forwarders), the path over every evaluated equal-cost path, the modeled policy, the destination’s listener and bind interface, for applications and services; the reverse direction as reverse routing and symmetry. | that the application accepts the connection, authentication, a TCP session, a stateful return decision, health and completion: runtime behaviour, which the simulation exchanges. |
| Path MTU | The largest packet that crosses each evaluated path unfragmented, and the payload that fits (TCP MSS, UDP or ICMP payload): the interfaces’ written MTUs, both ends of the cables on the way, tunnels as the largest inner packet their underlay leaves room for, with the encapsulation sizes the simulation’s packets have (the outer header of the tunnel’s family, a UDP tunnel’s UDP, the format’s header, ESP’s padding, VXLAN’s and Geneve’s inner Ethernet; nested layers inside out, each from its own identity: a layer carried over a relation between other addresses has that relation’s family), equal-cost branches and the return path apart. | an MTU that is not written (never taken as 1500: the result is then an upper bound; a tunnel interface without one takes what its underlay leaves room for); formats other than the one assumed per protocol (a GRE key, AES-GCM, Geneve options: a few bytes); a tunnel without a known format is taken as GRE and its limit called an estimate; a layer’s ends from a lease (a layer’s own ends are its relation’s static addresses); the size a flow actually uses (the simulation’s fragmentation, Fragmentation Needed / Packet Too Big and PMTUD show it). |
| Diagnosis | The answer to one communication question in order — its state (established, blocked, not completed with its cause not established, waiting, in progress, recovered, partial, cancelled, not established), the static and the runtime answer apart (finished or not, what was observed, whether its cause is established), what prevents or limits it with each distinct cause once and its messages, the evidence chain, the separate legs, the next actions — from the communication check and, once compared, the structured records of the run asked about (a send that carries the question — a host name’s in its family —, a client application’s own run with its retries when the question is its own communication, an MQTT client’s run by its own publications, each subscriber’s leg by the topics its filters ask for, those aged out of the records by the run’s tally): each message’s outcome with the device that answered (from the answer itself) and the reason it recorded, the drops of its exchange (decisive only when every attempt has one; the others contributing), its waits, retransmissions and DNS queries, the equal-cost branch taken, the recorded state changes behind a missing route (the routes the device found unusable then) or tunnel, a session’s silence by each message’s own drop; every piece of evidence a link to the exact record of its own simulation (a packet, an event, a policy rule as it was when diagnosed). | causes not recorded (said as not established, never guessed; a configured alternative never taken for what a route needed), coincidences in time as causes, a later state as the reason for an earlier outcome, a single root cause where several causes exist, records no longer kept or of an earlier simulation (said as unavailable), protocol-internal and TCP-sequence drops (no structured cause), QoS 2 and persistent MQTT sessions, a diagnosis of production networks. |
| Addressing | Each host address in its allocation state (configured, reserved, acquired in a snapshot, DHCP pool, nested network, unallocated); suggestions outside pools, reservations and used addresses; confirmed and possible conflicts in the scope the model establishes (a link-local address on its VLAN-scoped segment, any other in a VRF and a connected part), reuse the model separates, overlaps, addresses outside the declared networks. | addresses used outside the model, SLAAC interface identifiers in the configured model (a snapshot has them). |
| Service dependencies | Only what the model configures: application peers, MQTT brokers, resolvers, DHCP (a server on the client’s broadcast domain with a scope for it, or an IPv4 relay whose way passes the path, the policy and the listener both ways), timing sources, syslog senders and AAA clients; compared under a failure; a component’s Depends on, Used by and Failure affects. | dependencies nobody wrote down, business importance, DHCPv6 relays (DHCPv6 is served on the client’s link only), the remaining lease time of addresses already given. |
| Resilience: failures, outage impact, capacity | Single-component failures (each cable, device and LAG alone) with separate measures: requirements no longer satisfied, configured dependencies unavailable, devices disconnected, relations unavailable; outage impact of up to 64 components you choose (devices, cables, interfaces, relations; a group by its devices; a saved failure domain as an optional shortcut), compared with the same configured architecture without the outage, what was assumed told apart from what follows from it: dependencies, every saved expectation (availability and isolation), reachability of device pairs in a scope, and the stated traffic against the stated capacity, also without a failure (cables, an aggregate’s surviving members, shared radios; overload although still carried said apart). | business criticality, probabilities, production availability, protocol convergence, recovery times and transient loss (Experiments), combinations beyond the condition given, a hypothetical outage on a simulation snapshot, a network or an application unavailable on its own; throughput, queues, delay and hardware forwarding limits; a spread of traffic over equal-cost paths or bundle members (both an equal split and all on one path are evaluated). |
| Timing source paths | By the method asked for (PTP, NTP, or either: both reported). PTP: a source-capable clock of the domain and profile on the clock’s VLAN-scoped segments or behind boundary clocks. NTP: the configured source chain, upstream by upstream — each an address, reachable on UDP 123 (path, policy, listener), the device it is the one its traffic reaches — to a configured reference, with cycles, chains without a reference, upstreams outside the model and alternative roots said apart from a merely reachable upstream; a snapshot adds the synchronization the simulation observed. | accuracy (the simulation models the protocol states, not oscillators or clock discipline); precedence or bridging between NTP and PTP. |
| Saved experiments | An explicitly configured sequence run on the shared engine from its defined start (freshly booted, settled, or a cold start: every device with a power lifecycle booting; the entire model, its targets and their dependencies, or another scope), on scenario time: sends prepared from the communication’s identity, failures and restores, interface and power actions (with how long they last), joins and leaves, scenario-time multicast streams, applications; steps after an earlier action’s submission, an action waiting for its device to come up; observations of delivery, reception, MQTT delivery, device, interface and cable state, an address acquired, a neighbor resolved, a route, a protocol session, multicast membership, a timing state, a communication and the saved expectations, each over its window with the moment it was reached; played in the diagram with only its own traffic shown (its operations and their prerequisites); a run compared with the previous one. | real-time streams of Network events (they run on browser time); requirements it was not given (it never checks the architecture as a whole by itself); membership learned by a snooping switch; a state held for a period; convergence time, throughput and synchronization accuracy; a scripting language. |
| Simulation snapshots | The state of a running simulation at one moment for the analyses: leases, SLAAC and DHCPv6 addresses with their state, what is up, the routes learned. | later changes of the running simulation; hypothetical failures applied to it (they would blend two states). |

## Protocols: Layer 2

| Name | Level | Implemented | Not modeled |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ARP | Modeled behavior | Requests, replies and the ARP table with its timers are simulated before IPv4 unicast. | proxy ARP, ARP inspection. |
| NDP | Modeled behavior | Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement with the neighbour states (INCOMPLETE … PROBE); router discovery (Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement with prefixes, flags, lifetimes and DNS servers); SLAAC; duplicate address detection of every link-local, automatic and written global address (tentative until it passes; a duplicate is never used); default routers and their expiry. | SEND, proxy NDP, redirects, route information and router preference options, privacy addresses (identifiers come from the MAC), optimistic DAD. |
| Gratuitous ARP | Modeled behavior | Announcements when an interface comes up and when a redundancy group’s master changes are simulated. | ARP inspection or conflict handling beyond the log. |
| STP (RSTP) | Modeled behavior | A spanning tree per VLAN blocks loops; ports converge with the RSTP or STP timers and BPDUs are shown. | the tree is computed from the topology, not negotiated BPDU by BPDU; no MSTP regions. |
| LLDP | Modeled behavior | Periodic advertisements and each neighbour entry with its hold time are simulated. | their TLV contents. |
| CDP | Modeled behavior | Periodic advertisements and each neighbour entry with its hold time are simulated. | their TLV contents. |
| LACP | Modeled behavior | LACPDUs on every member (slow or fast rate), bundling and min-links are simulated; an aggregate bundles only members whose partner (its system and aggregate) is the same. | system and port priorities, standby links beyond the maximum. |

## Protocols: Routing

| Name | Level | Implemented | Not modeled |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OSPF | Modeled behavior | Hellos (their intervals, area and network type must match), the interface states with the DR and BDR election of RFC 2328 (priority 0, Waiting, non-preemptive), the adjacency states up to Full: the DBD exchange negotiates master and slave by router ID and rejects a DBD whose interface MTU is larger than its own (stuck in ExStart), then LSR, LSU, LSAck with retransmission; LSUs are taken only from a neighbour in Exchange or beyond; each router’s routes come from the records its OSPF LSUs brought it (flooded, acknowledged, sent again after 5 s), never from another protocol’s. | LSA types and contents field by field (a record per router: its OSPF adjacencies and its interfaces), DBD paging and the M bit (one DBD holds the database), area types and inter-area summarization, authentication. |
| IS-IS | Modeled behavior | IIHs, CSNPs, PSNPs and LSPs as frames on the link: the adjacency forms over the cable whatever the interfaces’ IP addresses, by the NET’s system ID and area and the level (level 1 only within an area, never with a duplicate system ID), with the three-way handshake and the holding time; each router’s routes come from the records its IS-IS LSPs brought it (an unnumbered interface: out of it to the neighbour’s own address; numbered interfaces in different subnets: no IPv4 next hop, said so). | LSPs field by field (a record per router), separate level-1 and level-2 databases and route leaking, the designated IS, authentication. |
| EIGRP | Modeled behavior | Hellos, the init Updates and their ACKs, the neighbour states with their hold time; a change is sent as a reliable Update, a lost neighbour as a Query that every other neighbour must answer with a Reply (one that has not after the 3 min active timer is reset: stuck in active); routes come from what its Updates and Queries brought, from neighbours that are Up. | DUAL’s feasibility condition and the Active hold of a route (another neighbour’s route is used at once), metrics from bandwidth and delay. |
| RIP | Modeled behavior | A distance vector: Responses carry prefixes and metrics (the router’s own with 0, through its export filter); a receiver adds the cost (1), takes a new prefix below 16, its neighbour’s new metric whatever it is (16: withdrawn) and another neighbour’s only when lower; split horizon with poisoned reverse; a route not refreshed for the timeout (180 s) is set to 16 and deleted after 120 s; an interface going down invalidates its routes at once; every change goes out in a triggered Response after 1 to 5 s, the whole table every 30 s; RIPv2 on UDP 520, RIPng on UDP 521 with its Responses from the link-local address (hop count 255 to ff02::9), checked on input. | authentication, hold-down timers, RIPv1, route tags beyond the origin carried for redistribution. |
| BGP | Modeled behavior | The session over a TCP connection of the transport, OPEN as structured parameters (AS checked, hold time negotiated, 0 for none), KEEPALIVE, the hold timer, NOTIFICATION and UPDATEs (taken only in Established); each router’s routes come from what its BGP UPDATEs brought it — never from another protocol’s floods — through the routing-policy subset (advertised prefixes, a default route, redistribution, ordered import/export filters, local preference, AS-path length and prepending). | NLRI field by field (an UPDATE carries the speakers’ records: their BGP sessions and interfaces), communities, MED, route reflection, iBGP split horizon, authentication. |
| LDP | Modeled behavior | Hellos, the session over a TCP connection of the transport (with its hold time) and its label mapping messages are simulated. | label-switched forwarding: traffic follows the IP path. |
| PIM | Modeled behavior | Hellos with the DR election, Join/Prune, Register and Register-Stop, the RPF check and multicast forwarding (sparse, SSM, dense) are simulated; each router uses its own RP (its static RP, its relations’ rp, else the candidate RP with the highest router ID among those whose Bootstraps reached it — each kept for its holdtime of 2.5 Bootstrap periods, then dropped — of the group’s address family). | a separate bootstrap router and C-RP-Advertisements (each candidate floods its own Bootstrap), BSR and RP priorities, group ranges per RP, Auto-RP, asserts. |
| IGMP / MLD | Modeled behavior | Reports, leaves, queries, the querier election and switches’ snooping per VLAN are simulated; every message with TTL 1 and the Router Alert option, its length by its version; MLD from the link-local address once valid (:: for a host’s Report before), the querier elected by link-local address; a message without Router Alert, or MLD from a global address, is ignored. | IGMP proxying, IGMPv1, source-specific queries. |
| BFD | Modeled behavior | Control packets with the three-way state machine; each end sends no faster than the peer takes, and detects after the peer’s multiplier × the slower interval (RFC 5880 §6.8.4, from what the Control packets say); a session down takes its client protocols down. | echo mode, demand mode, authentication. |

## Protocols: Services

| Name | Level | Implemented | Not modeled |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DNS | Modeled behavior | A relation’s demonstration queries cross the network; name resolution itself (A / AAAA, CNAME, forwarders, the resolver cache) is simulated from the DNS servers’ zones. | DNSSEC, TCP fallback, recursion beyond the model’s servers. |
| NTP | Modeled behavior | Client requests and server responses at the poll interval; each response carries the stratum its server knows (16: unsynchronized), and a client knows its upstreams only by those responses — synchronized to one that answered below 16, its stratum one more; a source answering 16 ends it at once, one silent for 8 polls (the reach register) too. | clock filtering, selection and discipline: no offset or accuracy is computed. |
| Syslog | Modeled behavior | Requests (and their answers) cross the network at a demonstration interval between the relation’s ends: reachability, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | message contents and the server’s application logic. |
| SNMP | Modeled behavior | Requests (and their answers) cross the network at a demonstration interval between the relation’s ends: reachability, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | message contents and the server’s application logic. |
| RADIUS / TACACS+ | Modeled behavior | Requests (and their answers) cross the network at a demonstration interval between the relation’s ends: reachability, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | message contents and the server’s application logic. |
| DHCP | Modeled behavior | DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST and ACK, relays, leases with renewal, rebinding and expiry are simulated from the servers’ scopes; DHCPv6 (stateful and stateless) on the server’s own link. | DHCPDECLINE, RELEASE, INFORM, option 82; DHCPv6 relays and prefix delegation. |
| CAPWAP | Modeled behavior | Requests (and their answers) cross the network at a demonstration interval between the relation’s ends: reachability, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | message contents and the server’s application logic. |
| HTTPS | Modeled behavior | TCP connections of the transport with the TLS 1.3 flights (ClientHello; ServerHello with the server’s Finished; the client’s Finished before its first request — the server takes no request before it), then requests and answers at a demonstration interval. | TLS itself: certificates, cipher negotiation and encryption are not checked; session resumption. |
| NetFlow / IPFIX | Modeled behavior | Requests (and their answers) cross the network at a demonstration interval between the relation’s ends: reachability, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | message contents and the server’s application logic. |

| DHCP server | Modeled behavior | IPv4 leases from its scopes (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST and ACK, through relays too, renewal, rebinding and expiry); DHCPv6 from its IPv6 scopes on its own link, stateful (Solicit, Advertise, Request, Reply, renewal) and stateless (DNS servers only). | DHCPDECLINE, RELEASE, INFORM, option 82; DHCPv6 relays and prefix delegation. |
| DNS server | Modeled behavior | Answers A and AAAA queries from its zones (the model’s DNS names and its own records), follows CNAMEs, asks its forwarders. | DNSSEC, zone transfers, TCP fallback. |
| NTP | Modeled behavior | Serves time on UDP 123 (its stratum, or one more than its upstream’s) and asks its upstreams at the poll interval; whether it is synchronized follows from their answers. | clock filtering, selection and discipline: no offset or accuracy is computed. |
| AAA | Modeled behavior | Its clients send authentication requests at a demonstration interval and get an answer (reachability and policy apply). | credentials and the shared secret are not checked; no accounting. |
| Syslog collector | Modeled behavior | Its senders send log messages at a demonstration interval (one way; reachability and policy apply). | message contents, severities and facilities. |
| Monitoring | Modeled behavior | ICMP probes and SNMP polls of its targets, with their intervals and timeouts, and each target’s up or down state. | MIB contents, traps, thresholds. |
| Proxy | Modeled behavior | Ends each client connection and opens its own to the upstream (a full TCP proxy), with its connect and client timeouts. | caching, HTTP semantics, TLS inspection. |
| Load balancing | Modeled behavior | Spreads connections over its healthy backends by its algorithm, with health checks, persistence and source NAT. | layer 7 rules, TLS offload. |
| VPN gateway | Configuration and validation | Its tunnels, remote-access pool and protected networks are checked; it forwards only to and from them. The tunnels’ own sessions are the IPsec / WireGuard / OpenVPN relations’. | remote-access client logins and their key exchange. |
| NAT | Modeled behavior | PAT, source NAT and destination NAT (port forwarding) between its inside and outside interfaces, with the translations for the replies. | ALGs, hairpinning, port-block allocation. |
| Wireless access | Modeled behavior | Each Wi-Fi network bridged to its VLAN, client association (its time), beacons and the idle timeout. | radio propagation, interference, roaming, the security handshake. |
| Wireless controller | Modeled behavior | The CAPWAP control channel to its access points (echo requests at the RFC 5415 interval). | firmware and radio management (channels, power). |
| Hypervisor | Modeled behavior | Its virtual switches with port groups and teaming, uplink failover, VMs powered with their host and restarted by HA. | live migration traffic, resource scheduling. |
| Container engine | Modeled behavior | Its container networks (bridge with NAT, host, macvlan, ipvlan, overlay), published ports and container start and restart. | orchestration, service discovery, overlay encapsulation details. |
| Storage service | Configuration and validation | Its protocols are checked and their ports (NFS 2049, SMB 445, iSCSI 3260) are open in the simulation, so tests and applications reach them. | NFS, SMB and iSCSI themselves. |
| PTP | Modeled behavior | PTPv2 of IEEE 1588-2008, its Default delay request-response profile over UDP/IPv4 multicast, two-step: Announce and the best master clock algorithm, Sync and Follow_Up, Delay_Req and Delay_Resp, port states, boundary clocks, end-to-end transparent clocks (residence time), the offset and path delay from the modelled timestamps. | clock accuracy is not verified: the estimates follow the modelled timestamps; no one-step, peer delay, gPTP / IEEE 802.1AS, other profiles, TSN, management messages, holdover quality. |
| MQTT broker | Modeled behavior | CONNECT / CONNACK (a second client with the same identifier takes over), SUBSCRIBE with + and # filters, the fan-out of each PUBLISH to the matching subscribers (QoS 0, QoS 1 with PUBACK and DUP retries), UNSUBSCRIBE, PINGREQ and the keep alive (1.5 ×), DISCONNECT; its sessions, subscriptions and counters. | QoS 2, persistent sessions (every session is clean), retained messages, wills, authentication, TLS and payload contents. |
| Applications | Modeled behavior | Each application’s profile: listeners, TCP and UDP clients, periodic messages, MQTT clients (see each profile); one that starts with the simulation starts once, when its device is operational; one outcome per original message, retries counted apart; Stop while its last message is on its way. | payload contents and application semantics: a name such as Modbus TCP labels it only. |
| Inspection | Modeled behavior | Traffic matching its block list is dropped inline or alerted on passively, with its inspection latency and fail-open or fail-closed. | signatures and protocol decoding beyond ports. |
| Domain separation | Modeled behavior | Only permitted transfers cross, by its implementation: a filtering bridge, a filtering router, or a protocol break with its transfer profiles. | content inspection of what it transfers. |

| Name | Level | Implemented | Not modeled |

| TCP listener (request/response) | Modeled behavior | Connections (the three-way handshake, retransmission, FIN) with a request and its answer of the sizes in effect cross the network: addressing, routing, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | payload contents and application semantics: a name such as Modbus TCP labels it, nothing of Modbus is simulated. |
| TCP client (request/response) | Modeled behavior | Connections (the three-way handshake, retransmission, FIN) with a request and its answer of the sizes in effect cross the network: addressing, routing, firewall policy and closed ports apply. | payload contents and application semantics: a name such as Modbus TCP labels it, nothing of Modbus is simulated. |
| UDP listener (request/response) | Modeled behavior | Datagrams (and their answers, for request/response) of the sizes in effect cross the network: addressing, routing, firewall policy and closed ports (ICMP port unreachable) apply. | payload contents and application semantics: a label names the application, its protocol is not simulated. |
| UDP client (request/response) | Modeled behavior | Datagrams (and their answers, for request/response) of the sizes in effect cross the network: addressing, routing, firewall policy and closed ports (ICMP port unreachable) apply. | payload contents and application semantics: a label names the application, its protocol is not simulated. |
| UDP receiver (one-way) | Modeled behavior | Datagrams (and their answers, for request/response) of the sizes in effect cross the network: addressing, routing, firewall policy and closed ports (ICMP port unreachable) apply. | payload contents and application semantics: a label names the application, its protocol is not simulated. |
| Periodic UDP messages (one-way) | Modeled behavior | Datagrams (and their answers, for request/response) of the sizes in effect cross the network: addressing, routing, firewall policy and closed ports (ICMP port unreachable) apply. | payload contents and application semantics: a label names the application, its protocol is not simulated. |
| MQTT client (publish / subscribe) | Modeled behavior | MQTT 3.1.1 over TCP: CONNECT / CONNACK, SUBSCRIBE / SUBACK with + and # filters, PUBLISH through the broker to the matching subscribers, QoS 0 and QoS 1 (PUBACK, DUP retries), UNSUBSCRIBE, DISCONNECT, keep alive with PINGREQ and reconnection (a periodic publisher goes on after it; a round that falls while not connected is skipped); packet identifiers 1–65535 per side, never one still in flight; topics and filters sized in UTF-8 bytes. | QoS 2, persistent sessions (every session is clean), retained messages, wills, authentication, TLS and payload contents. |
